categories.intro: The biggest source of silent bugs: Mid/InStr shift from 1-based to 0-based, while Len/Left/Right/NthField do not.

rules.name: Len(s) global form → s.Length (property)
rules.note: None — identical character count. Only syntactic: function call becomes a property (drop the parentheses).
rules.manual: Arguments containing nested parens/commas (e.g. Len(Mid(s,2))) are NOT matched by the identifier-only capture and are skipped; convert by hand: assign EXPR to a local String and use `local.Length`, or leave the deprecated `Len(EXPR)` in place. `(EXPR).Length` does not compile.
rules.caveat: Identifier-only capture avoids nested-call corruption. A user-defined method named Len would be rewritten — review. Matches inside string literals/comments containing 'Len('. \b prevents matching LenB or MyLen. RECEIVER SHAPE: the capture is identifier-only because Xojo has no member access on a literal or a parenthesised expression -- `"0123456789".IndexOf(c)` and `("00" + Hex(r)).Right(2)` are SYNTAX ERRORS, not style. So a skipped compound-argument call has exactly two outcomes: assign to a local and call the method on that, or leave the deprecated global in place. Writing the method form by hand is not a third option. See conversion-traps.md section 4 for which to prefer. IMPLICIT-CONVERSION TRAP: `EndOfLine` is a class, not a String. It converts implicitly in a string expression (`s + EndOfLine`), so `Len(EndOfLine)` looks like an ordinary identifier receiver and this rule rewrites it to `EndOfLine.Length` -- which does not compile. The working form is `EndOfLine.Native.Length`. Check any receiver that is a framework object rather than a String variable.

rules.name: s.Len method form → s.Length
rules.note: None — pure rename of a member name; identical value.
rules.caveat: Negative lookahead (?!\s*\() excludes any Len( call form; fixed-width lookbehind (?<=\.) requires a preceding dot. Still matches .Len inside comments/strings — review. \b prevents matching .LenB. ZERO IS NOT COMPLETION: this pattern is anchored on a literal dot, so it cannot see a receiverless call on the enclosing instance -- Xojo lets you write `Invalidate` for `Self.Invalidate`, and older code usually does. No match count from this rule is evidence that the member is fully converted. Finish with the bare-name sweep in phase 8 (`scripts/sweep.py`), which is the only pass that sees that form.

rules.name: Left(s, count) global form → s.Left(count)
rules.note: None — count is a quantity of characters, not a position. NO 1-based→0-based arithmetic. Pure structural rename of the global form to the method form.
rules.manual: A count argument containing a nested call (e.g. Left(s, Len(t)-1)) is NOT matched ([^,()] forbids parens/commas) — convert by hand: Left(SOURCE, COUNT) → SOURCE.Left(COUNT). This regex requires a comma inside the parens, so it only fires on the two-argument call form Left(x, y) and will NOT touch a bare .Left property read/assignment. STILL: a user method Left(a,b) would be rewritten, AND a two-arg call where the FIRST arg is itself a control's position used as a string (rare) is unlikely but possible. Matches inside comments/strings. The already-existing method form s.Left(n) is left alone (no global Left( token), which is correct. rules.name: Mid(s, start) global form, two-arg (no length), VARIABLE/EXPRESSION start → s.Middle((start)-1)
rules.note: 1-based → 0-based: the start position MUST be decremented by 1. The mechanical safe transform appends '- 1' to the captured start, producing source.Middle((start) - 1) — correct but ugly (e.g. (i+1) - 1), simplified by hand. Regex cannot do arithmetic. CONFIRMED against docs: Mid('This is a test', 6) and source.Middle(5) both yield 'is a test', so index N becomes N-1.
rules.manual: If the source OR start argument contains nested parentheses/commas (e.g. Mid(s, InStr(s,"x"))), the captures do not match and the call is SKIPPED — convert by hand: Mid(SOURCE, START) → SOURCE.Middle((START) - 1), then simplify the arithmetic. CAUTION: this two-arg rule matches only the no-length form because the second capture [^,()] forbids a comma; the three-arg form is a separate rule. After running, search for ') - 1' to simplify doubled offsets by hand. CRITICAL cross-statement caution: if 'start' is itself a former InStr result you are ALSO converting to 0-based IndexOf, the two -1s collide — see the dedicated 'InStr result used as a position' MANUAL rule.
rules.caveat: The second capture forbids commas so ONLY the two-argument Mid(source, start) matches. A user-defined two-arg Mid would be rewritten with an unwanted -1 — review. Matches inside comments/strings, producing a spurious '.Middle((x)-1)'. The (x+1)-1 ugliness is expected; flag for manual simplification. RECEIVER SHAPE: the capture is identifier-only because Xojo has no member access on a literal or a parenthesised expression -- `"0123456789".IndexOf(c)` and `("00" + Hex(r)).Right(2)` are SYNTAX ERRORS, not style. So a skipped compound-argument call has exactly two outcomes: assign to a local and call the method on that, or leave the deprecated global in place. Writing the method form by hand is not a third option. See conversion-traps.md section 4 for which to prefer.

rules.name: Mid(s, LITERAL start[, length]) — literal-aware variants (cleaner output)
rules.old: Mid(source, N[, length]) where N is a literal integer constant (1,2,3,...).
rules.new: source.Middle(N-1[, length]) with the decrement already applied as a clean literal.
rules.note: 1-based → 0-based. Because regex cannot do arithmetic, supply ONE find/replace pair PER literal value to get clean output (Middle(0), Middle(1), ...), avoiding the ugly (N) - 1 form.
rules.manual: This pattern handles only literal start = 1 (the common Mid(s,1) = 'from the beginning'). Enumerate only the literals your project uses (search Mid( to find them), or fall back to the variable rule and simplify by hand. NOTE: Mid(s,1) (whole string from start) could also simply become s without Middle at all, but Middle(0) is the safe literal transform.

rules.name: InStr(source, find) global form, two-arg (no start) → source.IndexOf(find)
rules.note: DOUBLE semantic change: (1) returned position 1-based → 0-based (every value now 1 lower); (2) not-found sentinel 0 → -1. Argument order for the two-arg form is unchanged (source→receiver, find first arg). Because the RETURN VALUE meaning changes, any consumer (> 0, = 0, >= 1, the position fed into Mid, etc.) MUST also be adjusted — see the comparison rules. Renaming InStr→IndexOf in isolation is a TRAP.
rules.manual: CRITICAL: do this rename ONLY after locating and fixing every comparison/use of the result. Recommended order: (1) search the whole project for \bInStr\b to inventory every call; (2) per occurrence, decide how the return value is consumed; (3) fix the consumer (>0→>=0, =0→=-1, position-into-Mid handling); (4) THEN rename. The two-arg find regex skips calls whose source/find contains nested parens/commas — convert those by hand. The three-arg leading-start form is a SEPARATE rule.
rules.caveat: VERY HIGH RISK if run blindly — silently leaves wrong index/sentinel semantics. VERIFIER CORRECTION: the extractor's source character class included a double-quote ([A-Za-z0-9_."]). That is DANGEROUS: for a string-literal source containing a comma, e.g. InStr("a,b", x), the capture would run 'a then stop at the comma and MISALIGN the split, corrupting the line. I REMOVED the quote from the class so a quoted-literal source is simply skipped (left for manual) rather than mis-split. User-defined InStr rewritten — review. Comments/strings matched. RECEIVER SHAPE: the capture is identifier-only because Xojo has no member access on a literal or a parenthesised expression -- `"0123456789".IndexOf(c)` and `("00" + Hex(r)).Right(2)` are SYNTAX ERRORS, not style. So a skipped compound-argument call has exactly two outcomes: assign to a local and call the method on that, or leave the deprecated global in place. Writing the method form by hand is not a third option. See conversion-traps.md section 4 for which to prefer.

rules.name: InStr/IndexOf result comparison: '... > 0' (found check)
rules.note: SENTINEL SHIFT: '> 0' (found, API1) must become '>= 0' (found, API2). If you rename InStr→IndexOf and leave '> 0', a match at position 0 (the first character — common!) is now WRONGLY treated as not-found. Silent correctness bug.
rules.manual: 1) Inventory: search the project for \bInStr\b. 2) For each occurrence decide how the result is consumed. 3) Found-check InStr(...) > 0 / >= 1 -> ...IndexOf(...) >= 0 (or <> -1). 4) Not-found InStr(...) = 0 / < 1 -> ...IndexOf(...) = -1 (or < 0). 5) If the result is stored in a variable, fix EVERY comparison of that variable. The GLOBAL form (InStr(s, x) > 0) has no global IndexOf, so convert it BY HAND to s.IndexOf(x) >= 0. METHOD-FORM ONLY semi-automated assist (verify each; the leading receiver lies outside the match and is preserved): Find (?<=\.)InStr\s*\(([^()]*)\)\s*>\s*0  ->  Replace IndexOf($1) >= 0.
rules.caveat: Any automated handling risks binding '> 0' to the wrong expression or matching a '> 0' belonging to a different value on the same line. The position-0 first-character match is the classic silent bug. Treat the whole InStr family as manual/review unless each consumer is individually verified.

rules.name: InStr result used directly as a 1-based position (e.g. into Mid/Middle)
rules.old: p = InStr(s, x) : t = Mid(s, p)
rules.note: Subtle: when an InStr result is consumed by ANOTHER index function you are ALSO converting to 0-based, the two -1 adjustments cancel — you must NOT double-decrement. If you mechanically apply '(p) - 1' inside Middle while p is already a 0-based IndexOf result, you introduce an off-by-one. rules.name: If db.Error / db.ErrorMessage check → Try/Catch DatabaseException (MANUAL — structural, multi-line)
rules.old: Database.Error As Boolean (set True after a failed call) and Database.ErrorMessage As String (the message). API 1 pattern (verified deprecated/recordset.md Edit/Update/DeleteRecord examples, lines 200-222, 401-410): call DB op, then 'If db.Error Then MsgBox(db.ErrorMessage)' or 'If Not db.Error Then ... rs.Update ... If db.Error Then ...'.
rules.new: API 2 Database has NO Error/ErrorMessage properties (VERIFIED: database.md properties table lists only DatabaseName, Host, Password, UserName). Every DB operation (Connect, SelectSQL, ExecuteSQL, AddRow, EditRow, SaveRow, RemoveRow, BeginTransaction, CommitTransaction, RollbackTransaction, and RowCount on unsupported DBs) RAISES DatabaseException. You catch it: 'Catch error As DatabaseException' and read error.Message (String) / error.ErrorNumber (Integer)
rules.note: FUNDAMENTAL shift from flag/return-code error handling to exception-based. The single-line regex engine CANNOT restructure across lines (Find is one line at a time and cannot wrap a preceding statement in Try ... Catch ... End Try). Worse, a regex that merely deleted or rewrote the 'If db.Error' line would leave the DB call UNGUARDED so a real failure crashes uncaught. MUST be done by hand.
rules.manual:
STEP 1 — FIND every site (RegEx on, Match Case off), Find-only (do not Replace): (a)  db\.Error   (b) \.ErrorMessage   (c) generally  \w+\.Error  and  \w+\.ErrorMessage  to catch any DB-variable name (mDB.Error, App.db.Error, conn.Error). STEP 2 — for EACH site, identify the DB call(s) the check guards (the SelectSQL/ExecuteSQL/AddRow/EditRow/SaveRow/RemoveRow/Connect/Commit/etc. statement immediately before the 'If db.Error' test, or the block an 'If Not db.Error Then' wraps). STEP 3 — wrap those calls in Try/Catch and delete the flag test. Template:

  API 1:
    rs = db.SQLSelect(sql)
    If db.Error Then
      MsgBox("DB Error: " + db.ErrorMessage)
      Return
    End If

  API 2:
    Try
      rs = db.SelectSQL(sql)
    Catch error As DatabaseException
      MessageBox("DB Error: " + error.Message)
      Return
    End Try

  API 1 (edit guarded by Not db.Error):
    rs.Edit
    If Not db.Error Then
      rs.Field("ProductName").StringValue = "Generic Widgets"
      rs.Update
      If db.Error Then MsgBox(db.ErrorMessage)
    Else
      MsgBox(db.ErrorMessage)
    End If

  API 2:
    Try
      rs.EditRow
      rs.Column("ProductName").StringValue = "Generic Widgets"
      rs.SaveRow
    Catch error As DatabaseException
      MessageBox("DB Error: " + error.Message)
    End Try

Mapping: db.ErrorMessage → error.Message (the Catch variable's property); db had no public numeric code but DatabaseException exposes error.ErrorNumber. MsgBox → MessageBox is a different category's rule. Fold in the SelectSQL/ExecuteSQL renames (separate rules) and remember RowCount now throws UnsupportedOperationException where RecordCount returned -1. STEP 4 — after converting, search again for any leftover \.Error  / \.ErrorMessage  on a database variable; remaining ones now reference non-existent members and will FAIL TO COMPILE — that compile error is the desired signal nothing was missed.
rules.caveat: N/A for regex (none provided). The risk being AVOIDED is exactly why this is manual: a naive regex on 'If db.Error Then' would either leave the DB call unguarded (silent crash on real errors) or match '.Error'/'.ErrorMessage' on unrelated objects (sockets, other exceptions, etc.). Hand-conversion confirms each site is a Database flag check and wraps the correct statements.

rules.name: New Date(year, month, day, ...) → New DateTime(...) (MANUAL — 7th-arg GMTOffset trap)
rules.old: New Date(Year, Month=1, Day=1, hour=0, minute=0, second=0)
rules.new: New DateTime(Year, Month, Day, hour=0, minute=0, second=0, nanosecond=0, timeZone As TimeZone = Nil)
rules.note: The first six parameters (Year, Month, Day, hour, minute, second) line up positionally between Date and DateTime, so a same-argument copy is correct for those — NO off-by-one on the date parts. BUT the 7th parameter differs in TYPE and MEANING: Date's 7th arg is GMTOffset As Double (HOURS from GMT, e.g. -7); DateTime's 7th arg is nanosecond As Integer and the TimeZone is the 8th arg. A blind rename of a 7-arg call silently reinterprets a GMT offset (e.g. -7) as 7 nanoseconds before — a TRAP. Also: Date defaults Month/Day to 1; DateTime's constructor does not, so 'New Date(2020)' must become 'New DateTime(2020, 1, 1)' with Month/Day supplied explicitly.
rules.manual: Find with \bNew\s+Date\s*\( (Match Case OFF, SEARCH only). Triage by argument count: (1) ONE to SIX args (Year through second, no GMTOffset) — the rename 'New Date(' → 'New DateTime(' is value-correct IF Month and Day are present; if the original relied on Date's Month/Day defaulting to 1 (e.g. 'New Date(2020)' or 'New Date(2020, 4)'), you must add the missing 1s because DateTime's constructor has no Month/Day defaults. Because arguments may contain nested parens/commas (e.g. New Date(Val(yr), mo, dy)), do this as review-each-match, never blind Replace-All. (2) SEVEN args (last is GMTOffset Double) — DO NOT rename verbatim. Put nanosecond=0 in slot 7 and a TimeZone in slot 8, converting hours→seconds: New DateTime(y, m, d, h, min, s, 0, New TimeZone(gmtOffset * 3600)) (TimeZone constructor takes gmtOffsetInSeconds As Integer — timezone.md). Verify each by hand.
rules.caveat: Argument lists frequently contain nested function calls and commas which defeat naive comma counting — count arguments by hand. Must not touch 'New DateTime('. Comment/string hits possible. The 7-arg verbatim rename compiles (7 valid args) yet is semantically wrong — silent corruption. Confirm whether the original relied on Month/Day defaulting to 1.

examples.b: Dim d As New Date(1956, 8, 13, 8, 23, 0, -7)  ' last arg is GMTOffset
examples.a: Var d As New DateTime(1956, 8, 13, 8, 23, 0, 0, New TimeZone(-7 * 3600))  ' nanosecond=0, offset→TimeZone in seconds
Var d As New DateTime(2020, 1, 1)  ' supply Month/Day; DateTime has no defaults for them

rules.name: Date property MUTATION (d.Year = …, d.Month = …, d.Day = …, d.Hour/Minute/Second = …) → reconstruct DateTime (MANUAL)
rules.forms: left-hand-side assignment form only (property on the LHS of '=')
rules.old: Assignment to a Date instance property: d.Year = v / d.Month = v / d.Day = v / d.Hour = v / d.Minute = v / d.Second = v
rules.new: No direct equivalent. DateTime is immutable (datetime.md lines 21-35, all read-only). Build a new DateTime via the Year/Month/Day Constructor (replacing the changed field) or via AddInterval/SubtractInterval / + /
rules.note: FUNDAMENTAL semantic break, not an index change. These compile and run on mutable Date but are ILLEGAL on immutable DateTime. A name-only type rename leaves these assignments as COMPILE ERRORS (loud, good) — but you must rewrite them. Often several sequential assignments (d.Year=…: d.Month=…: d.Day=…) collectively build one date and should collapse into a single 'New DateTime(year, month, day, …)'.
rules.manual: Find LHS assignments with the SEARCH-only regex \b(\w+)\.(Year|Month|Day|Hour|Minute|Second)\s*=(?!=) (Match Case OFF). The trailing =(?!=) restricts to a single '=' assignment and excludes the '==' comparison; you must still eyeball each hit to exclude '<=', '>=', '<>' (a read like 'x = d.Year' has the property on the RIGHT and is fine on DateTime — leave it). For each LHS hit: gather the full block of consecutive mutations on the same variable and replace the original 'New Date' + mutations with a single constructor call, e.g. 'Var d As New Date : d.Year=1954 : d.Month=2 : d.Day=10' → 'Var d As New DateTime(1954, 2, 10)'. If only one field changes relative to an existing DateTime, rebuild from its current parts: 'd = New DateTime(2000, d.Month, d.Day, d.Hour, d.Minute, d.Second)'. If the mutation is date arithmetic (e.g. d.Day = d.Day + 5), use AddInterval: 'd = d.AddInterval(0, 0, 5)'. Cannot be a single-line regex — it spans statements and needs restructuring.
rules.caveat: The find pattern must distinguish LHS (mutation, illegal) from RHS (read, fine). Reads such as 'total = d.Year * 12' must NOT be rewritten. Comment/string hits possible. GMTOffset, SQLDate, SQLDateTime, and TotalSeconds also have writable forms on Date but each has its own dedicated rule (different rewrites) — they are intentionally NOT in this pattern.

examples.b:
Dim d As New Date
d.Year = 1954
d.Month = 2
d.Day = 10

examples.a: d = d.AddInterval(0, 0, 5)  ' DateTime is immutable; AddInterval returns a new value

examples.b: Var yr As Integer = d.Year  ' read, on RHS
examples.a: Var yr As Integer = d.Year  ' unchanged — reads are fine on DateTime

rules.name: d.TotalSeconds → SecondsFrom1970 (EPOCH MISMATCH
rules.forms: both read (RHS) and write (LHS) forms — both are dangerous
rules.note: EPOCH SHIFT of exactly 2,082,844,800 seconds (1904-01-01 to 1970-01-01). DateTime.SecondsFrom1970 = Date.TotalSeconds - 2082844800. Consequences: (a) An elapsed-time DIFFERENCE (endTime - startTime) is SAFE because the constant cancels — but only if BOTH operands are migrated consistently. (b) Any ABSOLUTE use (persisting to file/DB, comparing to a stored 1904-based constant, feeding a constructor, displaying) is SILENTLY WRONG by 66 years after a name-only rename. (c) TotalSeconds is WRITABLE on Date; SecondsFrom1970 is READ-ONLY, so an assignment must become 'd = New DateTime(secs, TimeZone.Current)' (per datetime.md lines 153-157), adjusting secs for the epoch if it was stored on the 1904 basis.
rules.manual: Find every occurrence with \b\w+\.TotalSeconds\b (Match Case OFF, SEARCH only) and inspect each. Classify: (1) Pure elapsed difference 'd2.TotalSeconds - d1.TotalSeconds' where both ends are migrated DateTimes — rename both to SecondsFrom1970; the epoch constant cancels. Better: use DateInterval subtraction 'Var iv As DateInterval = d2 - d1' (datetime.md line 341, dateinterval.md). (2) Persisted/absolute value — either keep the original basis by adding the offset on write ('storedValue = dt.SecondsFrom1970 + 2082844800') and subtracting on read, OR migrate the stored data. Decide deliberately; do NOT just rename. (3) Constructing from seconds: replace the old write 'd.TotalSeconds = secs' (1904 basis) with 'd = New DateTime(secs - 2082844800, TimeZone.Current)' if secs is on the 1904 basis (drop the offset if it is already a 1970 value). (4) Any assignment 'd.TotalSeconds = x' is illegal on read-only DateTime — rewrite via the constructor. Never a safe blind Replace-All.
rules.caveat: The danger is the OPPOSITE of a typical false positive: the rename COMPILES and then yields values off by 66 years at runtime. Treat any automated rename of TotalSeconds as a defect. A user-defined property named TotalSeconds on a non-Date class would also be matched by the search pattern — confirm the receiver is a date.

examples.b:
Var startTime As Double = d1.TotalSeconds
Var endTime As Double = d2.TotalSeconds
Var elapsed As Double = endTime - startTime
examples.a:
Var startTime As Double = d1.SecondsFrom1970
Var endTime As Double = d2.SecondsFrom1970
Var elapsed As Double = endTime - startTime  ' SAFE: 1904↔1970 offset cancels in the difference
App.Prefs.Value("savedTime") = d.SecondsFrom1970 + 2082844800  ' keep 1904 basis for stored data, OR migrate the stored value and drop the constant
d = New DateTime(savedSeconds - 2082844800, TimeZone.Current)  ' DateTime is read-only; convert 1904→1970 basis

rules.name: d.GMTOffset (read or write) → DateTime.Timezone (MANUAL — no direct equivalent)
rules.note: Type and semantics change. Date.GMTOffset is a Double in HOURS and is writable (assigning shifts the stored instant). DateTime exposes a read-only Timezone of type TimeZone (not a number); offsets are in SECONDS when building a TimeZone. So to READ an hours offset, derive it: dt.Timezone.SecondsFromGMT / 3600. To SET it, construct a new DateTime with a TimeZone argument. There is no DateTime.GMTOffset, so a name-only rename fails to compile (loud) — but you still need the correct rewrite.
rules.manual: Find with \b\w+\.GMTOffset\b (Match Case OFF, SEARCH only). For a WRITE 'd.GMTOffset = -7': rebuild the DateTime with an explicit zone, e.g. 'New DateTime(y, m, d, h, min, s, 0, New TimeZone(-7 * 3600))' (offset in seconds; timezone.md confirms TimeZone Constructor takes gmtOffsetInSeconds As Integer). For a READ 'x = d.GMTOffset': replace with 'd.Timezone.SecondsFromGMT / 3600' to get hours. There is no single-line mechanical replacement; review each.
rules.caveat: GMTOffset does not exist on DateTime, so leaving it after a type rename is a compile error (loud, not silent). Comment/string hits possible. The read-side member is confirmed as TimeZone.SecondsFromGMT (Integer, seconds) per timezone.md — divide by 3600 for hours.

examples.b:
Dim d As New Date
d.GMTOffset = -7
examples.a: Var d As DateTime = New DateTime(DateTime.Now.Year, DateTime.Now.Month, DateTime.Now.Day, DateTime.Now.Hour, DateTime.Now.Minute, DateTime.Now.Second, 0, New TimeZone(-7 * 3600))  ' set zone via constructor; simplify as needed
Var offsetHours As Double = d.Timezone.SecondsFromGMT / 3600  ' TimeZone.SecondsFromGMT is Integer seconds

rules.name: Date display properties (ShortDate / LongDate / AbbreviatedDate / ShortTime / LongTime) → DateTime.ToString with FormatStyles (MANUAL)
rules.new: DateTime.ToString(loc As Locale, dateStyle As DateTime.FormatStyles, timeStyle As DateTime.FormatStyles) As String
rules.note: No index change; these properties simply DO NOT EXIST on DateTime, so a type rename leaves them as compile errors (loud). Mappings (per the FormatStyles table and ToString examples in datetime.md): ShortDate → ToString(Locale.Current, DateTime.FormatStyles.Short, DateTime.FormatStyles.None); LongDate → ToString(Locale.Current, DateTime.FormatStyles.Long, DateTime.FormatStyles.None) (Date used Full on Mac / Long on Windows per date.md line 134 — pick Long or Full to taste); AbbreviatedDate → (…Medium, …None); ShortTime → (…None, …Short); LongTime → (…None, …Long). Exact output depends on OS locale settings in both APIs.
rules.manual: Find each with \b\w+\.(ShortDate|LongDate|AbbreviatedDate|ShortTime|LongTime)\b (Match Case OFF, SEARCH only). Replace each with the corresponding ToString(...) call from the mapping above, substituting the receiver name. Although each mapping is a fixed string and could in principle be five separate regexes with the receiver as a backref, the result is verbose and LongDate needs a Long-vs-Full judgment, so do it as review-each-match. Caution: Date.SQLDate/SQLDateTime DO carry to DateTime by the same name (read-only) — handle those with the SQLDate rule, NOT here.
rules.caveat: Other classes may have properties named ShortDate etc.; confirm the receiver is a date. Comment/string hits possible. Do NOT lump SQLDate/SQLDateTime into this rule (they survive as same-named read-only properties).

rules.name: Date.SQLDate / Date.SQLDateTime assignment (write) → reconstruct via DateTime.FromString (MANUAL)
rules.forms: LHS assignment form (the write); reads need no change
rules.note: Semantic: on Date these are settable (assigning a SQL string parses and sets the date, raising UnsupportedFormatException on bad input); on DateTime they are READ-ONLY, and FromString raises a RuntimeException on bad input instead. A type rename leaves the WRITE as a compile error (loud). Reads are identical in name and need no change.
rules.manual: Find writes with the SEARCH-only regex \b(\w+)\.(SQLDate|SQLDateTime)\s*=(?!=) (Match Case OFF). The trailing =(?!=) restricts to a single '=' assignment and excludes '=='; still eyeball each to exclude '<=', '>=', '<>'. Reads like 'x = d.SQLDate' have the property on the right and are fine — leave them. For each write, rewrite 'd.SQLDate = s' → 'd = DateTime.FromString(s)' and change any exception handling from UnsupportedFormatException to RuntimeException. Reads require no edit.
rules.caveat: Must not touch reads (RHS). Note '==', '<=', '>=', '<>' are comparisons, not assignments; the =(?!=) guard plus manual inspection handles this. Comment/string hits possible.

examples.b:
Dim d As New Date
d.SQLDateTime = "2008-09-03 13:39:16"

examples.a: Label1.Text = d.SQLDate  ' unchanged — SQLDate read carries over to DateTime

rules.name: Date passed where a DateTime is needed → New DateTime(source As Date) conversion bridge (MANUAL)
rules.forms: interop/bridging form during a partial migration
rules.old: An existing Date object that must be handed to API 2 code expecting a DateTime (e.g. during a partial migration)
rules.note: No index change. This is the SAFE bridge when you cannot migrate a Date all at once: New DateTime(someDate) copies the instant correctly across the epoch difference (the framework handles the 1904↔1970 conversion internally — confirmed by datetime.md line 228-230). Use it instead of any hand arithmetic on TotalSeconds.
rules.manual: Nothing to find/replace mechanically; this is a tool to apply by hand where the type-rename and construction rules leave a genuine Date that must feed DateTime-typed code. Wrap the Date value: 'someDateTimeParam = New DateTime(theOldDate)'. Prefer this over any manual epoch math.
rules.caveat: None (manual insertion only). Just ensure the source variable is genuinely still a Date and not already a DateTime (passing a DateTime selects the Constructor(source As DateTime) overload — harmless copy, but unnecessary).

examples.b:
' theOldDate is still an API 1 Date; NewLogEntry expects a DateTime
NewLogEntry(theOldDate)

categories.intro: Return-code and error-flag checks become Try/Catch. Almost entirely manual — the regexes only locate occurrences.

rules.name: SocketCore.Error event handler mapped via AddHandler — add the new RuntimeException parameter (signature change)
rules.forms: both (the AddHandler statement that wires the method, and the bound method's own signature declaration on a different line)
rules.old: API 1 Error event had no exception parameter. A method bound with AddHandler looked like:
rules.note: Signature/arity change, NOT an index change. The handler method GAINS a trailing parameter (e As RuntimeException). A numeric code that API 1 read from a LastErrorCode property (or a passed Integer) is now e.ErrorNumber. If AddHandler's bound-method signature does not match the event's new signature the project will NOT compile — so an unfixed handler is a hard compile error (a loud failure, not a silent corruption), but a regex that fixes only ONE of the two coordinated sites (the AddHandler line OR the method declaration, never both, since they are on different lines) leaves the project non-compiling.
rules.manual: 1) LOCATE the wiring: RegEx ON, Match Case OFF, search  \bAddHandler\b[^,]*\.Error\s*,  to find every  AddHandler someSocket.Error, AddressOf SomeMethod  line. 2) For each, note the bound method name after AddressOf (or WeakAddressOf). 3) Open that method's declaration (a DIFFERENT line/item — the single-line engine cannot touch it from the AddHandler hit) and append a trailing parameter so it reads  (sender As <SocketType>, e As RuntimeException). 4) If the old method had a legacy Integer error-code parameter, replace its body uses with e.ErrorNumber and remove the Integer param. 5) In the body, replace any former code reference (the old Integer, or Me.LastErrorCode) with e.ErrorNumber. 6) SEPARATELY locate implemented (non-AddHandler) Error event handlers on socket subclasses: search  \bSub\s+Error\s*\(  and cross-check  \.ErrorNumber|LastErrorCode  to confirm the body reads the code from the new parameter. Two coordinated edits on different lines = cannot be one single-line regex; fix by hand.
rules.caveat: The locator matches .Error on ANY object with an Error event (sockets, controls, Database — see the Database rule), and matches inside strings/comments and commented-out AddHandler lines. The classic legacy body line  MessageBox(Str(Socket1.LastErrorCode))  must be hand-rewritten to e.ErrorNumber.ToString.

examples.b:
AddHandler MySocket.Error, AddressOf HandleSockError
...
Sub HandleSockError(sender As TCPSocket)
  MessageBox("Socket error " + Str(sender.LastErrorCode))
End Sub
examples.a:
AddHandler MySocket.Error, AddressOf HandleSockError
...
Sub HandleSockError(sender As TCPSocket, e As RuntimeException)
  MessageBox("Socket error " + e.ErrorNumber.ToString)
End Sub

examples.b:
Sub Error(errorCode As Integer)  ' implemented event in a TCPSocket subclass
  If errorCode = 103 Then ListBox1.AddRow("Address not resolved")
End Sub
examples.a:
Sub Error(e As RuntimeException)
  If e.ErrorNumber = 103 Then ListBox1.AddRow("Address not resolved")
End Sub
examples.note: The implemented-event form. This rule's Find covers the `AddHandler ... .Error,` form only; a `Sub Error(...)` event definition is found by its own signature and converted by hand.

rules.name: FolderItem.Delete → FolderItem.Remove (rename) AND drop the LastErrorCode check for Try/Catch IOException
rules.forms: method (the .Delete call) PLUS the associated LastErrorCode flag-check on OTHER lines
rules.new: Try : f.Remove : Catch error As IOException : … End Try. Remove is confirmed in folderitem.md (line 618-622) to raise IOException and to expose IOException.ErrorNumber / .Message / .Reason.
rules.note: Two coupled changes: (a) pure method rename Delete→Remove; (b) error detection moves from a post-call  If f.LastErrorCode > 0  test to a Catch IOException. A regex can mechanically do ONLY the rename. THE TRAP: if you rename Delete→Remove but leave the surrounding  If f.LastErrorCode > 0  in place, the code still COMPILES (LastErrorCode is merely deprecated, not removed) but the failure path is now DEAD CODE — Remove raises and unwinds before LastErrorCode is ever read, so the error handling silently never executes. Renaming without wrapping in Try/Catch is therefore unsafe; mark canRegex=false and force a manual hand-wrap.
rules.manual:
1) LOCATE every delete: RegEx ON, Match Case OFF, search  (\b[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*)\.Delete\b . 2) For each, confirm the receiver is a FolderItem (NOT a RowSet/RecordSet row, ListBox, array, or your own class with a Delete method) and check nearby lines for  \.LastErrorCode . 3) Rewrite to:
  Try
    f.Remove
    ' success-branch code that followed Delete
  Catch error As IOException
    ' code that was inside the old If f.LastErrorCode>0 block; use error.Message / error.ErrorNumber
  End Try
4) DELETE the now-dead LastErrorCode test. Because Try/Catch spans multiple lines the single-line engine cannot insert it; the .Delete→.Remove token swap could be auto-applied but you MUST still hand-wrap, so do not Replace-All.
rules.caveat: HIGH over-match: $1.Delete also matches RowSet/RecordSet .Delete (a real, different API), ListBox/array .Delete, Dictionary-style .Delete, and any user-defined .Delete method — none of which become .Remove. Also matches .Delete in strings/comments. Review each match; never blind Replace-All.

examples.b:
Dim f As FolderItem = GetFolderItem("Old.log")
f.Delete
If f.LastErrorCode > 0 Then
  MsgBox(Str(f.LastErrorCode))
Else
  MsgBox("File deleted!")
End If
examples.a:
Var f As FolderItem = New FolderItem("Old.log", FolderItem.PathModes.Native)
Try
  f.Remove
  MessageBox("File deleted!")
Catch error As IOException
  MessageBox(error.Message)
End Try
examples.note: Illustrates the whole error-code-to-exception migration around this rename, not the rename in isolation. The rule performs only the `.Delete` -> `.Remove` step.

rules.name: FolderItem.LastErrorCode flag check → Try/Catch IOException (locate-only; rewrite is manual)
rules.forms: property read (RHS of a comparison or assignment)
rules.new: No success-path property at all; wrap the operation in Try / Catch error As IOException and inspect error.ErrorNumber / error.Message / error.Reason (confirmed available per folderitem.md Remove description).
rules.note: Semantic move from a polled error flag to a thrown exception. The old folderitem error codes do NOT map to a guaranteed-identical IOException.ErrorNumber across platforms, so do not assume the same integers — prefer error.Message / error.Reason for user-facing text. There is NO 1-based→0-based / 0→-1 shift here; the change is purely control-flow.
rules.manual: LOCATE every occurrence: RegEx ON, Match Case OFF, search  \.LastErrorCode\b . For each: (1) confirm the receiver is a FolderItem (the same token is also valid on deprecated socket/Serial classes — do NOT assume IOException there). (2) Identify the file operation it guarded (usually the immediately preceding statement). (3) Wrap that operation in  Try … Catch error As IOException … End Try  and move the reporting code from the old  If …LastErrorCode <> 0  block into the Catch. (4) Replace any display of the numeric code with error.ErrorNumber.ToString, preferring error.Message for user text. (5) Delete the dead LastErrorCode test. Multi-line block = no single-line replacement; manual.
rules.caveat: .LastErrorCode is shared with deprecated socket classes and Serial (where it is NOT IOException), and the bare regex cannot tell the receiver type. Also matches strings/comments.

examples.b:
source.CopyTo(dest)
If source.LastErrorCode <> 0 Then
  MsgBox("Copy failed: " + Str(source.LastErrorCode))
End If
examples.a:
Try
  source.CopyTo(dest)
Catch error As IOException
  MessageBox("Copy failed: " + error.Message)
End Try

rules.name: BinaryStream.LastErrorCode / TextInputStream.LastErrorCode / TextOutputStream.LastErrorCode → exception handling (locate-only)
rules.new: Wrap Open/Create/Write/WriteLine in Try / Catch error As IOException (those methods raise IOException). There is NO LastErrorCode-equivalent property in API 2.
rules.note: Control-flow move to exceptions for OPEN/CREATE/WRITE failures only. CRITICAL non-obvious caveat: reading PAST the end of a stream still returns 0 / "" / False with NO exception — so a LastErrorCode check that was really detecting end-of-data must become an EndOfFile / BytePosition / Length check, NOT a Catch. You must decide per occurrence which case it was; converting an end-of-data probe into a Catch would silently lose the loop-termination logic.
rules.manual: LOCATE with  \.LastErrorCode\b  (RegEx ON, Match Case OFF). For each stream occurrence: (1) if it guarded an Open/Create/Write/WriteLine, wrap that call in  Try … Catch error As IOException … End Try  and move handling into the Catch; (2) if it was detecting end-of-stream / short read, replace with a loop using EndOfFile (e.g. Do Until inStream.EndOfFile) or compare BytePosition/Length — because over-read produces NO exception. Multi-line restructure; manual.
rules.caveat: The .LastErrorCode token is shared with FolderItem, sockets and Serial; the receiver type cannot be inferred from the bare property in regex. Strings/comments also match.

examples.b:
Dim bs As BinaryStream = BinaryStream.Open(f, True)
bs.Write(payload)
If bs.LastErrorCode <> 0 Then MsgBox("Write failed")
examples.a:
Try
  Var bs As BinaryStream = BinaryStream.Open(f, True)
  bs.Write(payload)
Catch error As IOException
  MessageBox("Write failed: " + error.Message)
End Try

examples.b:
Do
  data = data + inStream.Read(1000)
Loop Until inStream.LastErrorCode <> 0  ' was really detecting end-of-data
examples.a:
Do Until inStream.EndOfFile
  data = data + inStream.Read(1000)
Loop

rules.name: BinaryStream/TextInputStream ReadError (and WriteError) flag check → Try/Catch IOException OR EndOfFile (locate-only)
rules.new: Catch error As IOException for genuine I/O failures; for over-read use EndOfFile / BytePosition / Length (over-read does not raise).
rules.note: Control-flow change. CRITICAL distinction: an over-read returns 0/""/False with NO error and NO exception, so ReadError was historically often used as an end-of-data probe; in API 2 that case is handled by EndOfFile, NOT by a Catch. A blind 'wrap in Try/Catch' would silently lose end-of-data detection. Decide per occurrence.
rules.manual: LOCATE with  \.(ReadError|WriteError)\b  (RegEx ON, Match Case OFF). For each: confirm the receiver is a BinaryStream / TextInputStream (NOT a SQLiteBlob — that is the separate rule below, where the properties were REMOVED). If it followed an Open/Create or a Write that can fail (disk full, perms), wrap the operation in  Try … Catch error As IOException. If it was inside a read loop guarding end of data, convert the loop to  Do Until stream.EndOfFile … Loop  and delete the ReadError test. Multi-line; manual.
rules.caveat: SQLiteBLOB.ReadError/WriteError are a DIFFERENT case (REMOVED — see next rule); the bare regex cannot distinguish a SQLiteBlob receiver from a BinaryStream receiver. Also matches user properties named ReadError/WriteError and string/comment text.

examples.b:
Dim s As String = bs.Read(100)
If bs.ReadError Then
  MsgBox("Read failed")
End If
examples.a:
Try
  Var s As String = bs.Read(100)
  ' use s
Catch error As IOException
  MessageBox("Read failed: " + error.Message)
End Try   ' NOTE: if this was really detecting end-of-data, use 'If bs.EndOfFile Then' instead — over-read does not raise.

examples.b:
Do
  chunk = bs.Read(1000)
Loop Until bs.ReadError   ' really an end-of-data probe
examples.a:
Do Until bs.EndOfFile
  chunk = bs.Read(1000)
Loop

rules.name: SQLiteBLOB.ReadError / SQLiteBLOB.WriteError → IOException (properties REMOVED — must be deleted, locate-only)
rules.old: blob.ReadError / blob.WriteError checks after blob.Read / blob.Write. Confirmed by updating_older_projects.md line 113-115: SQLiteBLOB 'now raises an IOException on any Read/Write errors (instead of you having to check the ReadError/WriteError methods to see if they are True).'
rules.new: Wrap blob.Read / blob.Write in Try / Catch error As IOException. There is NO ReadError/WriteError property in API 2
rules.note: Pure control-flow move to exceptions; no index change. Unlike BinaryStream, these properties are GONE on SQLiteBlob, so an unfixed reference eventually fails to compile (loud failure) rather than silently no-op.
rules.manual: LOCATE with  \.(ReadError|WriteError)\b  then CONFIRM the receiver is a SQLiteBlob (look for a nearby OpenBlob / SQLiteBlob declaration). Rewrite the surrounding read/write loop into  Try … Catch error As IOException … End Try  and DELETE the  If blob.ReadError / If blob.WriteError  test entirely. NOTE: SQLiteBlob's end marker is EndOfFile (API 2), not the API 1 EOF — verify the loop condition was modernized too. Multi-line; manual.
rules.caveat: Shares the token with BinaryStream/TextInputStream ReadError (which STILL exists) — you must inspect the receiver type. Matches strings/comments.

examples.b:
While Not blob.EOF
  data = data + blob.Read(1000)
  If blob.ReadError Then
    MsgBox("Error reading from BLOB.")
    Exit While
  End If
Wend
examples.a:
Try
  While Not blob.EndOfFile
    data = data + blob.Read(1000)
  Wend
Catch error As IOException
  MessageBox("Error reading from BLOB: " + error.Message)
End Try

rules.name: Database.Error / Database.ErrorCode / Database.ErrorMessage flag checks → Try/Catch DatabaseException (cross-ref Database category; locate-only)
rules.forms: property reads (db.Error in a condition; db.ErrorCode / db.ErrorMessage in the body)
rules.new: Try : <db operation> : Catch error As DatabaseException : … error.ErrorNumber … error.Message … End Try. Confirmed databaseexception.md exposes ErrorNumber (Integer) and Message (String).
rules.note: Control-flow move. Note the property RENAME inside the handler: the old db.ErrorCode value is now error.ErrorNumber on DatabaseException (the word changes Code→Number — VERIFIED: databaseexception.md has ErrorNumber, not ErrorCode); db.ErrorMessage becomes error.Message. No numeric/index shift. This overlaps the Database category — defer the authoritative SQLExecute→ExecuteSQL / SQLSelect→SelectSQL / RecordSet→RowSet renames to THAT category; here handle only the error-flag detection.
rules.manual: LOCATE three tokens (RegEx ON, Match Case OFF): the flag  \b[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*\.Error\b  (this also finds socket .Error and control .Error — review each), plus  \.ErrorCode\b  and  \.ErrorMessage\b . rules.name: As Text -> As String (FLAG: deprecated-type swap, not a pure synonym)

rules.new: As String -- the API 2 String datatype
rules.note: SEMANTIC RISK confirmed from api/deprecated/text.md: Text is deprecated in favor of String and 'Text values automatically convert to String' -- so the value-level conversion is automatic (less dire than 'distinct, no conversion'). rules.name: `FolderItem.Item(i)` → `ChildAt(i-1)` (1-based→0-based)
rules.old: f.Item(Index As Integer) As FolderItem  ' Index is one-based
rules.new: f.ChildAt(index As Integer) As FolderItem  ' index is zero-based
rules.note: 1-based→0-based index shift. Item's array starts at 1; ChildAt starts at 0, so every index drops by one. The mechanical patch wraps the index as ChildAt((expr) - 1), but a manual loop rewrite is cleaner: `For i = 1 To f.Count … f.Item(i)` becomes `For i = 0 To f.Count-1 … f.ChildAt(i)`. Like Item, ChildAt resolves aliases by default (followAlias defaults to True) and may return Nil.
rules.manual: Prefer rewriting the enclosing loop rather than leaving ChildAt((i) - 1). Change `For i = 1 To f.Count` … `f.Item(i)` to `For i = 0 To f.Count - 1` … `f.ChildAt(i)`. For a single call like f.Item(1), simplify ChildAt((1) - 1) to f.ChildAt(0). The regex only matches a single-argument call with no nested parens/commas; calls whose index expression itself contains parentheses or a comma must be converted by hand.
rules.caveat: `.Item(` is a very common member name on other types (e.g. Dictionary, XmlNode, MenuItem-style collections, and user-defined classes), so this fires on any `.Item(...)` regardless of receiver type and will wrongly apply the -1 shift to non-FolderItem receivers. Step through with Replace & Find and confirm each receiver is a FolderItem. Also matches `.Item(...)` inside string literals/comments. ZERO IS NOT COMPLETION: this pattern is anchored on a literal dot, so it cannot see a receiverless call on the enclosing instance -- Xojo lets you write `Invalidate` for `Self.Invalidate`, and older code usually does. No match count from this rule is evidence that the member is fully converted. Finish with the bare-name sweep in phase 8 (`scripts/sweep.py`), which is the only pass that sees that form.
